transcript.content: Hi, welcome in—thanks for coming. To start off, can you tell me what brings you in today?

Uh… they sent me from the station. I guess I was doing something they didn’t like.

I was moving the airway bags around—putting them in the right pattern—and saying the dispatch numbers out loud. My lieutenant told me to stop, but I… I couldn’t just step away. It felt like if I broke it, the whole bay would go bad.
When you think about it now, do you feel that fear is probably excessive or not quite right, or do you feel certain that something bad really would happen if you didn't arrange things that way?

I don’t know… it didn’t feel excessive then.

I felt pretty sure the bags had to be in that pattern, and the numbers had to be said right. If I stopped when he told me to, it felt like the whole bay would go bad somehow. I know that sounds… off, but at the time I couldn’t step away.
How long have you been feeling this need to arrange things in that exact pattern and say the numbers out loud—days, weeks, or longer?
I guess… longer than days. Maybe around two months. The camera and paperwork stuff, and then the station thing… it’s all kind of been happening in that stretch.
Have you noticed or heard anything unusual—like sounds, voices, or visions—that others don't seem to notice, around the time these urges to arrange things happen?
I… don’t know. I haven’t really noticed voices or visions or anything like that. It’s more just… the feeling that it has to be done a certain way.
Have you had any recent head injuries, illnesses, seizures, or other medical problems around the time these urges started?
Not that I can think of. I mean… I haven’t had a head injury or anything like that. No seizures that I know of. Nothing medical that really stands out around then.

When you feel the urge to arrange the bags or say the numbers, do you see it as your own thought that you try to resist, or does it feel like something happening to you that you can't really call your own?

It feels like… mine, but not really something I can just ignore. Like at the station, with the airway bags, I knew the pattern was the right one, and if I stopped saying the dispatch numbers or stepped away, it felt like the whole bay would go bad. So when my lieutenant told me to stop, I just… couldn’t break it.

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient exhibits recurrent, intrusive urges to arrange objects (airway bags) in a specific pattern and to vocalize dispatch numbers, which he recognizes as his own thoughts/impulses (ego-syntonic but distressing) rather than externally imposed. He reports magical thinking ('if I stopped, the whole bay would go bad') indicating a compulsive belief driving repetitive behavior, with impaired insight at the time of the episode though some ability to reflect afterward ('I know that sounds off'). These compulsions have persisted for about two months, causing significant occupational impairment (reprimanded by his lieutenant, inability to stop despite direct order). No hallucinations, delusions, or thought insertion were endorsed, ruling out a primary psychotic disorder (F20.9). No dissociative symptoms (e.g., amnesia, identity disturbance) were reported, making F44.9 unlikely. No medical, neurological, or substance-related etiology was identified. The clinical picture—intrusive urges, compulsive rituals, magical thinking, and impaired but present insight—best fits Obsessive-Compulsive Disorder (F42).
